1918.352.title: Kora
1918.352.tech: Gourd, wood, rawhide, string, and rope
1918.352.dims: Diameter: 32.4 cm (12 3/4 in.); Overall: 111.8 cm (44 in.)
1918.352.desc: The kora is an instrument that has 21 strings. This example is now missing many, which would have been tied along its long neck. The strings are plucked with the fingers, causing the sound to resonate in the half-sphere-shaped gourd body. Stitch marks on the back show that many cracks on the gourd were repaired in the past.

1918.346.title: Sitar
1918.346.tech: Gourd and wood with pigment, ivory, and bone; copper alloy: frets; iron alloy: strings (with one modern copper replacement)
1918.346.desc: The stringed instrument known as the sitar usually provided the central sound for the musical performances that were a constant feature of court life in India. A sitar, unlike a vina, has movable frets, which are raised metal strips across the fingerboard. When their position is moved, the pitch of the notes changes. The size of the gourd on this small sitar was selected to resemble an ostrich egg, the material used for novelty sitars during the 19th century. They were mainly for display and played only on rare occasions by a woman or child. Bengal was a center for the production of decorative instruments.

1918.371.title: Guqin made by Zhang Ruixiu of Suzhou
1918.371.tech: Seven-string Asian long zither, chordophone, made from wood, lacquer, mother of pearl, and silk strings
1918.371.desc: China’s most prestigious instrument, the guqin can be traced to the Chu culture almost 2500 years ago. By the late Ming dynasty, Jiangnan was a center of high-end guqin production. Coated in black lacquer, this elegantly crafted instrument is inscribed on the inside, stating it was made by Zhang Ruixiu of Suzhou for Mr. Tianchi of Haiyu, also known as Yan Cheng (1547–1625). Yan was a key figure in guqin music history and founder of the Yushan school in Suzhou. Zhang Ruixiu was a guqin maker, known for achieving a supreme tone quality. Ten instruments attributed to him are known, of which this guqin has the earliest date.

1929.343.title: Drum (ngoma)
1929.343.dims: Diameter: 31.2 cm (12 5/16 in.); Overall: 40 cm (15 3/4 in.)
1929.343.desc: This musical instrument takes its name ngoma from the Kongo language word for "drum." Specialized craftspeople often made these drums. The wooden base is hollow and covered with a first hide, then a second one held tight by plant fibers. This allows the sound to resonate when just the first membrane is struck. In Uganda, drums contain a ritual "heart" known only to its maker, which helps to imbue it with power. In contrast with royal drums (mpango), this instrument is not considered sacred. The sounds from men striking drums could be used as a kind of communication or as music in a performance setting.
